conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been vomiting since 5 a.m. I haven’t eaten anything, and it’s just watery. I also have a headache and felt chills earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had episodes like this before, right? Does this feel similar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly like before. It’s the same pattern—nausea, then vomiting, and I just can’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The nurses mentioned you sometimes make yourself vomit because it helps you feel better. Is that true?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… when I drink water or ginger ale, I feel worse unless I bring it up. It gives me some relief, even if it’s not normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But repeatedly inducing vomiting can cause serious problems—like electrolyte imbalances, damage to your esophagus, or even heart issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize it was that dangerous. I just do it because it feels like the only thing that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work on safer ways to manage that urge. For now, we’re going to keep you on IV fluids and give you medications to help with nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. My blood sugar’s probably high too, since I haven’t eaten but I’m still vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your glucose was 395 when you arrived. We’ve given you insulin and fluids to help correct that. We’ll keep monitoring it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My blood pressure’s always high during these episodes too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s 158/86 now, and your heart rate is elevated. That’s likely from the stress, vomiting, and maybe not absorbing your blood pressure meds because you’re vomiting them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I take metoprolol and lisinopril at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart those once you can keep oral meds down. For now, we may need to give you IV blood pressure medication if it stays high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been doing this for years—doctors always say it’s my diabetes or gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You do have type 1 diabetes and a history of gastroparesis, but your recent gastric motility study was normal. That makes us think this might not be purely a stomach-emptying issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering that anxiety or a functional disorder might be playing a big role. The fact that you feel better after inducing vomiting suggests a behavioral component.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do get really anxious during these episodes. But it’s hard to tell what comes first—the nausea or the anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They can feed into each other. We’re going to start you on Ativan for anxiety, which may also help with nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never taken that before. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s commonly used for anxiety and nausea. We’ll start low and only use it as needed. We’re also increasing your citalopram dose to 20 mg daily to help with mood and anxiety long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I haven’t vomited since last night, and I didn’t make myself do it either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. Your labs are improving—your white count was high yesterday at 12.3, but it’s down to 9.8 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. High white counts can happen with stress, vomiting, or dehydration. It’s coming down now that you’re more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. My throat’s been a little sore too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning an EGD tomorrow to look into your stomach. We may do another botox injection, which has helped you before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I want to do that. It helped last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, we’ll take biopsies during the EGD to check for inflammation or infection, especially since your throat is sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Sometimes people with diabetes get esophageal candidiasis. We’ll start fluconazole just in case, even before the biopsy results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ll take it as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from your EGD. The procedure went well. You received botox in the stomach, which may help reduce vomiting episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Did they see anything unusual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endoscopist saw areas that looked like candidiasis, so biopsies were taken. But preliminary report says no fungal infection was found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why do I have a sore throat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy did show inflammation and an ulcer, but no fungus or virus. We’ll keep you on fluconazole for now and discuss with your PCP whether to continue after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m glad the botox was done. I hope it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve kept down clear liquids and now a soft diet. Your blood pressure is also much better—150/70 today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger. I haven’t had the urge to vomit, even when I drink water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’re going to advance you to a regular diet today. We’re also restarting your regular meds by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about the Ativan and fluconazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take Ativan as needed for anxiety or nausea for the next four days. Fluconazole for four days total—then talk to your PCP about continuing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had no vomiting for two days, your labs are stable, and you’re eating well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. Should I see my psychiatrist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we strongly recommend psychiatric follow-up. We’re giving you a letter with resources for counseling and relaxation techniques.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make the appointment. I want to stop this cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the right step. Also, please don’t induce vomiting—it can lead to serious complications like heart rhythm issues or esophageal tears.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I promise I’ll try. Thank you for helping me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. You’re alert, eating well, and your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with updated meds: citalopram 20 mg daily, Ativan as needed, and fluconazole for four days. Continue your regular diabetes and blood pressure meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’ll follow up with GI and my PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and please schedule psychiatric follow-up. We’re here if anything changes, but we expect you’ll continue improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
